You learn the present subjunctive (hable, coma, viva, sea, tenga…) and use it to say what you want or hope SOMEONE ELSE will do: quiero que, espero que, ojalá.
the bride and groom, the engaged couple
the groom / the bride; boyfriend / girlfriend
to marry, to get married to
I want you to come to my wedding.
I hope the weather is nice.
I hope it all goes well!
Mum would rather we got married in May.
To understand WHAT the subjunctive is and why it exists (a wish, not a fact).
To form the present subjunctive of regular verbs (-ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a).
To form the subjunctive of the basic irregular verbs: ser, estar, ir, tener, hacer, venir, decir, poder, saber.
To use quiero que / espero que / prefiero que / te pido que + subjunctive.
To use ojalá + subjunctive for wishes.
Ana and Mihai are back from Japan, engaged. On Sunday, at lunch, Ana’s mother Carmen already has a thousand ideas for the wedding.
Well, darling, when’s the wedding? I want you to tell me right now.
Mum, we’ve only just got back from Japan. We haven’t decided anything yet.
Well, I’d prefer you to get married in May. The weather’s lovely in May and the flowers are gorgeous.
That sounds fine to me. But my parents live in Romania. I hope they can come.
Of course they’ll come! And I want your mother to stay with me. That way we’ll get to know each other.
Mum, we don’t want a very big wedding. We want it to be something simple, with family and friends.
Simple? Darling, Aunt Pepa is expecting us to invite her. And the cousins from Seville. And the neighbours…
How many guests is that, roughly?
Two hundred! Mum, please don’t invite the whole of Madrid, I’m begging you.
All right, all right. But I want you to wear your grandmother’s wedding dress. She’s kept it since 1965.
Grandma’s dress? Mum… I’d really love that.
And I want Kenji to be my best man. Without him we’d never have met at the club.
Very good. And the food, who’s making it?
If only Kenji and Sofía could cook it together: a bit of Japan, a bit of Italy and a bit of Spain.
An international banquet… All right. But I hope there’s paella too.
And sarmale. My mother will never forgive me if there are no sarmale.
Goodness, what a strange family we’re going to be! …Be very happy, children.
“hace buen tiempo” = the weather is nice
“nos conocemos” = we get to know each other
“no nos habríamos conocido” = we wouldn’t have met
“vamos a ser” = we’re going to be
The stress stays where it was in the present: HA-ble, CO-ma, VI-va. In “nosotros” it moves to the second-to-last syllable: ha-BLE-mos, co-MA-mos.
o-ja-LÁ, with a rough j (like the ch in Scottish “loch”) and the stress on the last syllable. It comes from Arabic: “if God wills”.
Three short forms you’ll hear all the time: A-ya, BA-ya, SE-a. In “haya” the h is silent.

Until now you’ve spoken almost only in the INDICATIVE: the mood of real facts (como, comí, comeré). The SUBJUNCTIVE is the mood of things that are NOT facts but wishes, hopes, emotions, doubts, possibilities.
Sé que vienes. (I know you’re coming.)
Quiero que vengas. (I want you to come.)

English barely shows the subjunctive (“If I WERE you”), so Spanish needs a new habit: where English says “I want YOU TO come” (object + infinitive), Spanish says “quiero QUE VENGAS” (que + subjunctive). After “want / hope / prefer + someone else”, think: que + subjunctive.
2. How to form it: the “opposite vowel” rule
Take the first person singular of the present (yo hablo), drop the -o and add the “opposite” vowel: -ar verbs take -e, -er / -ir verbs take -a.
You’ve seen these forms before! The negative imperative (no hables, no comas) and the usted imperative (hable, coma) ARE subjunctive forms (chapter 23).
Because you start from “yo”, the irregularities of the present are kept: tener → yo tengo → tenga; hacer → hago → haga; decir → digo → diga; poner → pongo → ponga.
3. The six irregulars to learn by heart
Six verbs don’t follow the rule, because their “yo” doesn’t end in -o (soy, estoy, voy, he, sé, doy):
Memory trick: “SEA, ESTÉ, VAYA, HAYA, SEPA, DÉ”. Repeat it 5 times like a poem.
4. Quiero que + subjunctive: wishes about SOMEONE ELSE
The golden rule: if the person who wants and the person who acts are the SAME, use the infinitive. If they are DIFFERENT people, use que + subjunctive.
Quiero que vayas. (I want you to go.)
Prefiero que os caséis en mayo.

The typical English speaker’s mistake: “Quiero tú ir” or “Quiero que vas” (indicative). Correct: Quiero que vayas. After quiero que / espero que / prefiero que / te pido que, ALWAYS use the subjunctive.
Verbs that work the same way: querer, esperar, preferir, desear, pedir, necesitar, aconsejar, recomendar.
Ojalá (from Arabic: “if God wills”) expresses a strong wish. It is ALWAYS followed by the subjunctive, with or without que:
I hope it’s sunny on the wedding day!
I really hope your parents can come.
Is Kenji coming? — I really hope so!
Other good wishes with the subjunctive: ¡Que tengas suerte! (Good luck!), ¡Que te mejores! (Get well soon!), ¡Que aproveche! (Enjoy your meal!), ¡Que seáis felices! (Be happy!).
I hope your parents can come.
I want Kenji to be my best man.

Ana and Mihai write the text of their wedding invitation together. Here’s the first draft, full of wishes.
After four years of Spanish lessons, Japanese lessons, karaoke and lots of cups of tea, we’ve decided to get married.
The wedding will be on Saturday 17 May, at twelve o’clock, at Madrid Town Hall. Afterwards there will be a reception in the garden of Kenji’s restaurant.
We want all of you to come, those who live nearby and those who live far away.
We’re not asking you to bring presents. We only ask you to bring the desire to dance.
To those of you coming from Romania and Japan: we hope the journey isn’t too tiring. We’ll pick you up at the airport.
To Grandma Rosario: this time, please close the window before you make the cocido.
Please confirm your attendance before 1 April. We really hope you can be with us on the happiest day of our lives.
“ganas de” = the desire to, feel like
En el jardín del restaurante de Kenji
¿Qué piden Ana y Mihai a los invitados?
¿Qué le piden a la abuela Rosario?
Three weeks before the wedding, Mihai’s mother, Elena, arrived in Madrid. It was the first time she had left Romania.
She had two huge suitcases. One was for clothes. The other was full of food: cheese, cold meats, jars of zacuscă and a bag of flour “because in Spain it surely isn’t the same”.
Carmen was waiting for her at the airport with a huge sign: “BUN VENIT, ELENA” (Welcome, Elena). She had written it in Romanian with Mihai’s help, but it had two mistakes.
The two mothers looked at each other. Neither spoke the other’s language. Elena knew a little French; Carmen, a little English.
For a few seconds nobody said anything. Mihai and Ana looked at each other, nervous. “I hope they get on,” thought Ana. “I hope there isn’t a war,” thought Mihai.
Then Carmen opened her arms and gave her two kisses. Elena, who was expecting a handshake, laughed and gave her three, the Romanian way.
At Carmen’s house the real adventure began. The next day Elena got up at six and went straight to the kitchen.
When Carmen woke up, the house smelled of onion, meat and cabbage. Elena was making sarmale for two hundred people.
“But the wedding is in three weeks!” Carmen said with gestures.
“Sarmale… freezer…” Elena answered, pointing at the fridge.
Carmen didn’t want a guest to work in her house, but she didn’t know how to tell her. So she did the only possible thing: she put on an apron and started helping her.
For three weeks the two mothers cooked together every morning. Carmen taught her to make potato tortilla. Elena taught her to make cozonac.
They talked with their hands, their eyes and a translation app Ana had installed for them. Sometimes the app translated very strange things, and the two of them laughed for minutes on end.
One day the app translated “zacuscă” as “food for the bears’ winter”. Carmen couldn’t stop laughing all afternoon.
But not everything was easy. One afternoon they argued about the menu. Carmen wanted jamón on every table. Elena wanted ciorbă as the first course.
“Soup in May? It’ll be hot!” said Carmen.
“No ciorbă, no wedding!” said Elena in Romanian, and Carmen understood perfectly without a translation.
In the end, Kenji solved the problem. He suggested a small bowl of cold ciorbă, “like gazpacho, but Romanian”. The two mothers looked at him suspiciously… then said yes.
On the night before the wedding, Ana found the two mothers in the kitchen, sitting with a cup of tea each and the grandmother’s dress between them.
Elena had hand-sewn a small blue flower on the inside of the dress, where nobody could see it.
“It’s a tradition from my village,” she explained to Ana, with the app. “So that the bride is never sad.”
Carmen’s eyes were full of tears. She took Elena’s hand and said softly, in the little Romanian she had learned:
Ana left the kitchen without a sound. In the hallway, she called Mihai.
“What’s happened? Have they argued again?” he asked, worried.
“No,” Ana answered, smiling. “I think tomorrow it isn’t just two people getting married. It’s two families.”
And from the kitchen came the two mothers’ laughter. The app had just translated “cuscru” (your child’s father-in-law) as “the enemy’s father”.
¿Qué traía Elena en la segunda maleta?
Con las manos, los ojos y una aplicación
¿Cómo resolvió Kenji la discusión del menú?
Con una ciorbă fría, como un gazpacho
¿Para qué cosió Elena una flor azul en el vestido?
Para que la novia nunca esté triste
